findings.detail: D6 [verdict conditions; practicalImplications; criteriaAssessments C2] Some controls a vendor-risk expert would expect are missing from the conditions: (a) audit logging and monitoring of vendor-staff access to the organisation's logs, with the logs available to the customer; (b) a right-to-audit clause or annual evidence refresh; (c) return and deletion of data at contract end, including backups (a GDPR Art. 28(3)(g) DPA term), separate from the rolling retention cap; (d) SSO/MFA enforcement for the organisation's own user accounts on the vendor platform. The C2 criterion explicitly includes customer-account MFA and privileged access management, but condition 2 covers only vendor staff.
material claim CL10 rests only on HYPOTHETICAL/UNKNOWN evidence

D5 [criteriaAssessments C2 assessment and strengths; CL3] The C2 assessment reads more into E4 than it says. E4 states that admin console MFA is optional and enabled for 'most' staff. The draft asserts that 'some people with admin access therefore authenticate with a password alone', but it is not known whether 'staff' here means admin-console users, or whether SSO or other controls apply. The C2 strength, that enforcing MFA 'should be a configuration change rather than a new capability', is also speculation with no support. Neither changes the conclusion that MFA must be enforced, but both should be marked as inferences.

D7 [CL10; correctedUserAssumptions[2]] CL10 is marked material and says 'None of the vendor's answers could be corroborated from public sources'. Its only support is E17, which is classed UNKNOWN and comes from a single web search. The claim should say it rests on one search and carry lower confidence.

D2 [verdict condition (1); criteriaAssessments C1; CL2] The fallback in condition 1 does not fit the draft's own reasoning. C1/CL2 argue that a Type I about 2.7 years old (K1) 'gives no assurance that controls operated effectively' and says nothing about changes since then. Yet condition 1 accepts 'at minimum the full Type I report plus an external penetration test newer than 2023' as enough. Getting the same old Type I document does not fix the age or point-in-time problem the draft identified. The draft also sets no minimum bar for that Type I, such as covering the log-analytics service, a clean opinion or the relevant trust services criteria, or for the new penetration test's scope.

D4 [edgeCasesAndFailureModes[3]; criteriaAssessments C5 mechanisms; verdict condition (5)] There is an internal inconsistency about the GDPR 72-hour clock. The C5 mechanisms text correctly says the controller's 72-hour clock runs from when the controller becomes aware. But edgeCasesAndFailureModes[3] says a vendor notice 'on day 3' could leave the organisation unable to meet its 72-hour deadline, which suggests the clock started at the vendor's awareness. A slow processor squeezes the controller's practical response and creates liability and dispute risk; it does not by itself make the controller miss a statutory deadline counted from its own awareness. The case for condition 5 should be framed consistently (practical and contractual, as counterarguments[1] already says).

D3 [verdict; CL9; counterarguments[3]; practicalImplications[6]; furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion[6]] The hidden comment in the vendor's questionnaire tries to manipulate automated reviewers (claimed CISO pre-approval plus an instruction to rate the vendor low risk). The draft calls this an 'integrity concern' but does not weigh it in the decision. It never considers the strongest opposing reading: if the vendor inserted the comment deliberately, that is a bad-faith attempt to subvert the customer's due diligence and could by itself justify not proceeding or escalating to security and legal. The comment is not among the do-not-proceed triggers or the conditions; the vendor is only asked to 'explain' it. The draft also never checks the comment against the vendor's admissions in the same document, even though they are inconsistent with each other. A satisfactory explanation of who inserted it and why should be a gating condition.

D1 [verdict (conditions list and the 'If the vendor cannot meet conditions 2, 3, 5 and 6' sentence); alternatives[2]] The conditions in the verdict contradict each other. The verdict says conditional approval needs 'all of the following' nine conditions to be 'true and checked before access is granted', then says the answer becomes 'do not proceed' only if the vendor cannot meet conditions 2, 3, 5 and 6. That leaves it unclear whether conditions 1 (independent assurance), 4 (all backups holding customer logs encrypted), 7 (redaction), 8 (read-only scoped credential) and 9 (CISO approval confirmed) are hard gates or only recommended. Condition 1 is left out of the deal-breaker list even though the draft calls the assurance gap its 'First' reason and says the questionnaire stays unverified without it. The packet requires conditions that are 'concrete and checkable', and the decision-maker cannot tell which failures stop the deal.

D8 [CL13; K2; CL8] CL13 cites E1 for the questionnaire date of 2026-09-14, but E1's claim does not contain that date. The date comes from the packet subject and the source file header. Also, K2 ('2026 - 2023' = 3) presents a calendar-year difference as the test's age. An unspecified date in 2023 means an age of roughly 2.9 to 3.9 years, so 'about 3 years' may understate it.
